strengths: The paper targets a practical and relevant problem (open-vocabulary understanding of 3DGS scenes) and offers a genuinely training-free alternative to the dominant per-scene contrastive optimization paradigm, which is a meaningful engineering contribution.

Quantitative results are strong: SOTA mIoU on LERF object selection (54.3 vs. 43.6 for Dr.Splat) and on ScanNet segmentation across 19/15/10 classes, against a comprehensive set of recent baselines (OpenGaussian, InstanceGaussian, Dr.Splat, LangSplat, etc.).

The efficiency gains are substantial and well-documented (Table 1): eliminating per-scene optimization, reducing CLIP feature storage from ~3GB to ~3MB, and lowering peak VRAM, addressing a real deployment bottleneck of prior work.

The pipeline is logically decomposed (mask lifting via back-projection, entropy/opacity-based neutral point filtering, VLM-based textual distillation), and each component is supported by an ablation (Tables 4-5), with the feature extraction ablation (36.9 -> 54.3) clearly justifying the VLM design choice.

The paper is generally well-written and clearly structured; the neutral point concept (boundary Gaussians that are neither foreground nor background) is an interesting and plausible observation about 3DGS representations.
weaknesses: The 'polysemy' claim is central to the motivation and title ('Polysemous Language Gaussian Splatting'), but no experiment actually validates polysemous representation. The method stores a set of VLM-generated candidate names per object, yet the LERF/ScanNet evaluations measure standard mIoU, not multi-concept retrieval. The claimed advantage over 'one-to-one' assignments is asserted rather than demonstrated.

There is a significant confound in the comparisons: the method uses Gemini 2.5 Pro (a very large, closed-source commercial VLM) to name objects, while all baselines rely only on CLIP. Gains may largely reflect the vastly stronger language/grounding capacity of the external model rather than the proposed grouping mechanism. The paper claims to be 'VLM-agnostic' but does not ablate across weaker/open VLMs, so the generalization of the core contribution is unclear.

Reproducibility is a concern: no code release is mentioned; key hyperparameters (top-N views, similarity threshold η, thresholds τ_h and τ_α, prompt text, granularity levels) are not specified; and results depend on a proprietary, potentially non-deterministic VLM whose outputs may change over time.

Evaluation breadth is limited: LERF contains only four scenes, and ScanNet evaluation reuses the scene/class splits of OpenGaussian. There are no experiments on other 3DGS semantic benchmarks, no test of robustness to the acknowledged SAM/DAM2SAM failure modes, and no failure-case analysis beyond two brief limitation statements.

The neutral point processing ablation shows a small net effect (53.0 -> 54.3, with entropy filtering alone only +0.2), which raises questions about how much of the headline improvement comes from this technically novel component versus simply using a much stronger VLM for naming.

The efficiency comparison in Table 1 somewhat obscures costs: the method still requires SAM + DAM2SAM segmentation/tracking over all frames plus VLM API calls per object, whose runtime and monetary cost are not reported; 'hours to minutes' claims in the abstract are not precisely substantiated in the text.

Some presentation issues: Eq. (4) notation has an undefined 'b' exponent/term; typos ('After that, We leverage'); and the paper conflates semantic segmentation of whole objects with texture-level queries, given that grouping operates at object level (Fig. 2 refers to 'object' groups) while LERF queries include part-level concepts like 'bear nose' — how the framework resolves part-level semantics within a group is not explained.

strengths: The paper targets a practical and timely problem: eliminating costly per-scene contrastive optimization for point-level open-vocabulary understanding in 3DGS. The efficiency claims are substantiated by Table 1, showing zero scene optimization time, ~3MB feature storage (vs ~3GB), and ~8GB peak VRAM (vs ~20-28GB) for competitors.

Empirical results are strong on both benchmarks: 54.3 mIoU on LERF object selection (surpassing the best pixel-based method, 51.4, and best point-based method, 43.6) and consistently best results on ScanNet across 19/15/10-class settings (Table 3).

The neutral point processing idea (semantic entropy over multi-view labels plus an opacity-based filter) is a reasonable and somewhat novel mechanism for handling ambiguous boundary Gaussians, and Table 5 shows the VLM-based feature extraction ablation yields meaningful gains (50.1 to 54.3 over filtered image matching).
The overall pipeline is clearly written and easy to follow, with a well-structured method section, motivating figures, and ablations covering both the grouping and feature extraction components.
weaknesses: The 'training-free' framing is somewhat misleading. The pipeline depends on SAM, DAM2SAM, and, most critically, Gemini 2.5 Pro — a very large, proprietary, closed-source VLM — to generate object identity hypotheses. The heavy computational and capability burden is effectively outsourced to a foundation model orders of magnitude larger than what baselines use (CLIP only). This raises fairness concerns about the comparisons in Tables 2 and 3, and the claim of 'uncompressed CLIP representations for linguistic precision' understates the reliance on VLM-generated text priors.

The claimed polysemy contribution is weak. Multi-concept semantics arise simply because the VLM outputs a list of candidate names per object, which is a thin mechanism to support the 'polysemy-aware' framing in the title and abstract; no experiment specifically evaluates or demonstrates multi-concept queries (e.g., 'wooden' or 'furniture' retrieval behavior).

Potential evaluation contamination: using a powerful generative VLM to name objects in widely known benchmarks (LERF, ScanNet with standard scene/category splits from OpenGaussian) risks leakage of benchmark conventions, and the paper provides no analysis of VLM sensitivity, prompt ablations, or results with alternative (open-source) VLMs despite claiming the framework is 'VLM-agnostic'.

Several important details and costs are unreported: query-time latency (the VLM step could dominate the 'minutes' claim for adaptation but per-query cost matters too), the search threshold η and its sensitivity, the value of fixed thresholds τh and τα, and how performance degrades under tracking/segmentation failures — the robustness claims in §3.1 are asserted but not tested.

The neutral point processing ablation (Table 4) shows a marginal total gain (53.0 to 54.3), with entropy filtering alone contributing only +0.2, so the headline mechanism is weakly supported and the improvement is within a plausible noise range given no variance or significance reporting.

Novelty is moderate: lifting 2D masks to 3D Gaussians via rendering-weight back-projection is established practice (e.g., GS-Grouping, Lifting-by-Gaussian-style pipelines), and the main new elements are the opacity-based filtering heuristic and the VLM naming step.

Reproducibility is a concern: no code release is mentioned, and results depend on a proprietary VLM whose outputs may change over time. The ScanNet protocol also disables Gaussian densification, a nonstandard choice whose interaction with baselines (which may or may not use identical settings) is not clarified.
The limitations section is thin, acknowledging only SAM mask errors and occasional VLM mislabeling, without addressing the deeper fairness/dependency concerns above.

strengths: The core idea is compelling and well-motivated: replacing expensive per-scene contrastive feature optimization with a direct mask-lifting + matching pipeline is a meaningful paradigm shift for point-level open-vocabulary 3DGS understanding, and the empirical gains are substantial (54.3 mIoU on LERF vs. 43.6 for the previous best point-based method; 45.5 mIoU on ScanNet 19-class vs. 40.7).

The efficiency results are a major practical contribution (Table 1): no per-scene training, ~3MB feature storage versus ~3GB for baselines, and ~8GB peak VRAM versus 20-28GB. Reducing scene adaptation from hours to minutes is valuable for real deployment.

The technical design is sensible and clearly explained: the rendering-consistent back-projection weight (Eq. 2-3) is principled, the two-stage neutral point filtering (multi-view label entropy + opacity-based disambiguation of solid vs. transitional points) is a neat and novel mechanism, and VLM-based semantic distillation addresses the known CLIP view-variance problem in a simple, robust way.

The ablations are targeted and support each component: Table 5 shows VLM text matching (54.3) substantially outperforms single-view (36.9), averaged (39.2), and even filtered image-feature matching (50.1), and Table 4 shows the two filtering stages are complementary.

The paper is generally well-organized, with a clear taxonomy of prior work (pixel-based vs. point-based; training-based vs. projection-based), and limitations are honestly acknowledged in the conclusion.
weaknesses: The central 'polysemy' claim is under-supported. The abstract and introduction repeatedly emphasize polysemy-aware representation, but the method essentially assigns a set of candidate names per object group via a similarity threshold η, and no experiment specifically evaluates multi-concept semantics (e.g., a desk point retrievable as 'desk', 'wooden', and 'furniture'). Since each Gaussian still belongs to at most one object group (or the neutral set), the point-level polysemy claim is more architectural marketing than demonstrated capability.

Reproducibility is a significant concern. The paper relies on a closed-source, proprietary VLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro) whose version, prompt, and output variability make exact replication difficult, and key hyperparameters are never given: the entropy threshold τh, opacity threshold τα, matching threshold η, and the number of top-N views are all said to be fixed but their values are not reported. No code release is mentioned.

The VLM's runtime and monetary cost are unquantified. The efficiency argument (Table 1) counts training time and CLIP storage but omits the cost of VLM API calls per object, which could be nontrivial in object-dense scenes; the comparison would be fairer with this included.

There is a potential technical inconsistency in the neutral point identification: foreground/background weights W1/W0 (Eq. 3) use occlusion-aware splatting weights, but the multi-view binary labels used for entropy (Eq. 4) appear to be computed by projecting Gaussian centers into masks without a visibility/occlusion check, so points hidden behind an object could be spuriously labeled foreground. This is not discussed.

Evaluation breadth is narrow: LERF has only 4 scenes and ScanNet uses the same scene/category subsets as OpenGaussian. Table 2 shows the method does not beat the best pixel-based method on every scene (e.g., teatime: 64.4 vs. LangSplat's 65.1; ramen: 45.6 vs. GOI's 52.6), so the 'surpasses SOTA pixel-based approaches' framing should be softened; also, related training-free pixel-based work (e.g., FlashSplat, cited but not compared) is absent from the comparison.

The neutral point ablation gain is modest (Table 4: 53.0 → 54.3, with entropy filtering alone contributing only +0.2), so the mechanism, while elegant, has limited measured impact relative to the narrative weight it receives.

Details of the candidate-name generation are thin: the number of candidate names, how the predefined prompt is constructed, and how failures cascade (poor SAM masks or VLM hallucinations, acknowledged in Sec. 5) are not characterized quantitatively, making it hard to judge robustness.

strengths: The extrinsic (decoupled) paradigm is well-motivated and clearly articulated: shifting the semantic unit from individual Gaussians to object groups addresses genuine weaknesses of the embedding paradigm (storage bloat of GBs of features, semantic ambiguity at boundaries, and the inability of a single feature vector per Gaussian to express polysemy). The ~25% multi-category point statistics in Sec. 10.2 empirically support the polysemy motivation.

Efficiency gains are substantial and well-documented: no per-scene optimization, ~1000x reduction in semantic feature storage (3MB vs ~3GB), ~8GB peak VRAM vs ~20-28GB for baselines, and a full component-wise runtime breakdown (Tab. 9) showing ~9 minutes vs hours for training-based alternatives.
Genuine state-of-the-art on ScanNet 3D semantic segmentation (Tab. 3): 45.5/47.2/53.7 mIoU consistently exceeds InstanceGaussian, Dr.Splat, LAGA, and LUDVIG across 19/15/10 class splits.

Thorough and unusually honest experimental analysis: ablations on neutral point thresholds (Tab. 8), number of VLM prompts (Tab. 7), VLM choice (Tab. 6, showing performance is bounded by the VLM), sparse-mask robustness (Fig. 7), failure cases (Sec. 9), and real-world/Grasp-Net validation beyond the two standard benchmarks.

The neutral point concept (semantic entropy over multi-view labels + opacity-based filtering) is a clean, lightweight contribution with quantified gains (53.0 -> 54.3 mIoU) and analysis of the complementary failure modes of each filter alone.
weaknesses: Overclaimed headline result on LERF. The text states the method 'achieves a new state-of-the-art result, outperforming the previous best-performing method by 3.9 mIoU' (Sec. 4.1), but the paper's own Table 2 shows LAGA at 64.0 and 3DVLGS at 62.0 mean mIoU, both well above the reported 54.3. The 3.9 gain holds only relative to LUDVIG within the '3D Training-free' subset, which is not stated. On the paper's primary object-selection benchmark, the method is not SOTA and trails the best baselines by ~10 mIoU; the claim must be substantially qualified.

Limited technical novelty of the core pipeline. SAM-mask back-projection to group Gaussians, multi-view mask tracking (here via SAM2/DAM2SAM), and attaching object-level semantics to point groups are all established ingredients (e.g., Gaussian Grouping [31], GS-Grouping [31] cited, and closely related training-free works such as 'Gaga: Group Any Gaussians' (arXiv 2024) that appear uncited and unbenchmarked). The main novelty is framing (extrinsic paradigm) plus the VLM-naming step, which is a straightforward design choice; the missing comparison to the most similar training-free grouping works weakens both novelty and empirical positioning.

A conceptual limitation of replacing continuous features with VLM-generated nouns is not analyzed: attribute-level queries (color, state, texture, spatial relations — e.g., 'red cup', 'teapot with bear nose', 'coffee in a glass') cannot be matched by cosine similarity against noun hypotheses except via loose association. The paper reports strong results on such fine-grained queries (Figs. 3, 5) without explaining how five nouns per object capture these attributes, or which queries fail for this structural reason.

Potential evaluation-protocol concern: the task definition says 'the most similar instance(s) are selected' (Sec. 4.1), but the method description (Eq. 6, Sec. 3.5) uses a hard cosine-similarity threshold (eta = 0.9) rather than argmax. Threshold-based matching vs. ranking-based baselines is not apples-to-apples, and 0.9 is a very high CLIP text-text similarity threshold whose sensitivity is not reported for this parameter (unlike tau_h, tau_a, and prompt count).

Reproducibility is weakened by dependence on a closed-source, proprietary VLM: the best result (54.3) uses Gemini 2.5 Pro, while the strongest reproducible configuration (InternVL3-78B) scores 50.2 — within noise of LUDVIG (50.4). The SOTA margin is thus contingent on a proprietary model. Also, 'Scene Opt.' is marked 'None' for Dr.Splat/LUDVIG while the reported savings narrative centers on avoiding optimization, so the differentiation from existing training-free methods rests mainly on storage.

Multi-granularity grouping details are underspecified: how 'scene'-level masks are used, how conflicting granularities are resolved during querying, and the cost/behavior when objects are heavily overlapping or occluded are not analyzed quantitatively (only qualitatively via Grasp-Net).

strengths: The core idea of decoupling geometry from semantics via an extrinsic index layer (object groups + lightweight textual hypotheses instead of per-Gaussian feature vectors) is sensible and practically motivated; the efficiency gains are substantial and well-documented (Table 1: ~3MB CLIP storage vs ~3GB for baselines, no per-scene optimization, lowest VRAM footprint; Section 8 runtime analysis).

The ScanNet semantic segmentation results (Table 3) show consistent improvements over all compared point-based baselines (45.5/47.2/53.7 mIoU vs. best prior 40.7/42.5/50.8), with a reasonable protocol reusing OpenGaussian's scenes and categories.

The supplementary material is unusually thorough: sensitivity analysis of neutral-point thresholds (Table 8), VLM-choice ablation (Table 6), prompt-count ablation (Table 7), sparse-mask robustness (Fig. 7), failure case analysis (Fig. 12), and component-wise runtime breakdown (Table 9), which supports reproducibility of the experimental design.

Clear writing overall; the neutral-point concept (entropy-based multi-view disagreement filtered by opacity) is a simple but well-motivated mechanism, and the ablation (Tables 4, 8) supports both filtering stages.
weaknesses: Overstated SOTA claim: the text (Sec. 4.1) states the method 'achieves a new state-of-the-art result, outperforming the previous best-performing method by 3.9 mIoU' on LERF, but Table 2 shows LAGA (64.0) and 3DVLGS (62.0) and Occam's LGS (61.3) all exceed Ours (54.3). The 3.9 gain holds only over LUDVIG (50.4) within the training-free subset. The claim as written is misleading and only indirectly qualified by table grouping.

Limited novelty: the pipeline is largely an assembly of existing components — SAM/DAM2SAM multi-view mask tracking, mask back-projection for 3D grouping (closely related to Gaussian Grouping [31] and GS-Grouping), and VLM-generated object names matched via CLIP text features. The 'extrinsic paradigm' framing repackages known ideas; 'neutral points' is acknowledged (Sec. 10.1) to overlap with prior 'boundary point' work [15, 34], and the reported gain from neutral-point processing is modest (53.0 to 54.3 mIoU).

Heavy dependence on a proprietary VLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro) as a core component harms reproducibility and makes the results non-stationary: the VLM ablation (Table 6) spans 47.0-54.3 mIoU, meaning roughly a quarter of the reported margin over LUDVIG is attributable to VLM choice. The method also inherits SAM/VLM failure modes, as the authors themselves document (Sec. 9, Fig. 12).

The approach converts open-vocabulary querying into matching against a small closed set of VLM-proposed nouns (five per object, threshold η=0.9). This limits genuinely open-ended semantics: queries phrased differently from the VLM's vocabulary, attributes, or relational descriptions ('duck on the Rubik's Cube') fall outside the index, and only a few such qualitative examples are shown without quantitative attribute/relation evaluation.

Evaluation breadth is narrow: two datasets, both popular in this line of work; the LERF protocol is 2D multi-view IoU rather than true 3D evaluation, and per-scene processing is still ~9.25 minutes for a single complex scene (Table 9), which is favorable vs. training-based baselines but far from the 'zero scene adaptation' impression given in Table 1.
Presentation defects: broken LaTeX artifacts remain in the camera-ready text (e.g., '\label{eqw}' and raw markup in Eqs. 1-4), which suggests insufficient proofreading.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly articulated: shifting semantics from per-Gaussian feature embedding to an external, object-level index layer that references geometry, which directly addresses real limitations of the embedding paradigm (storage bloat, per-Gaussian feature entanglement, boundary ambiguity).

The efficiency contribution is substantial and well-documented: training-free operation, ~3MB vs ~3GB CLIP feature storage, ~8GB peak VRAM, and ~9 minutes end-to-end vs hours for baselines (Tables 1 and 9), with a useful component-wise runtime breakdown.
Strong quantitative results on ScanNet semantic segmentation (45.5/47.2/53.7 mIoU across 19/15/10 classes, Table 3), clearly ahead of prior point-based methods including training-free LUDVIG.

Thorough supplementary analysis: VLM choice ablation, prompt-count sensitivity, neutral-point threshold sensitivity, robustness to sparse mask supervision, failure-case analysis (Fig. 12), and the viewpoint-inconsistency analysis of CLIP image features (Fig. 14) provides good evidence for design choices.
The paper is honest about limitations (SAM mask quality dependence, occasional VLM mislabeling) and includes qualitative comparisons on real-world and complex scenes (Figs. 9, 10).
weaknesses: Overclaimed result on LERF: Section 4.1 states the method 'achieves a new state-of-the-art (SOTA) result, outperforming the previous best-performing method by 3.9 mIoU,' but the paper's own Table 2 shows LAGA at 64.0 mean mIoU versus Ours at 54.3, and 3DVLGS (62.0) and Occam's LGS (61.3) also exceed it. The 3.9 gap corresponds only to LUDVIG among training-free methods. The method is SOTA only within the training-free category, which materially weakens the headline accuracy claim and should be stated accurately.

The accuracy gain from the paper's most distinctive technical component, neutral point processing, is small: the ablation (Table 4) shows 53.0 -> 54.3 mIoU (~1.3), and the opacity filter alone degrades performance (52.6). The contribution of the multi-granularity/polysemy mechanism is not directly ablated on benchmarks where polysemy matters.

Semantic matching rests entirely on a small set of VLM-generated nouns (five) scored with a high CLIP text-text threshold (η=0.9). This limits expressiveness for texture- or attribute-level queries (e.g., 'blueberry nose') and for selecting partial object regions not covered by the generated hypotheses; the paper's claims about fine-grained queries are supported mostly by selected qualitative examples rather than systematic evaluation.

Reliance on proprietary components (Gemini 2.5 Pro, DAM2SAM) and no mentioned code release raise reproducibility concerns, although the appendix ablations with open VLMs (InternVL3-78B) partially mitigate this.

Novelty of the 'extrinsic paradigm' framing is somewhat overstated: object-level grouping via SAM-mask back-projection is well-established (e.g., Gaussian Grouping/GS-Grouping), and replacing visual features with text hypotheses is an incremental, though sensible, design; the positioning as a new paradigm versus an efficient pipeline choice is debatable.

Presentation issues remain: a visible LaTeX artifact in Eq. (1) ('\label{eqw}'), minor typos, and the mismatch between the abstract's categorical claims ('outperforms established embedding-based frameworks') and the actual ranking in Table 2 require careful revision.
